meta.title: Gap-Fill: What Standing Waves Do + Satellite Transponder Power Sharing
meta.source_content: RF-Hub original — topic-gap fill from PO's own Intermediate exam experience (topic-gap analysis only; no exam wording reproduced)

questions.section_name: Standing Waves, SWR, and the Reflection Coefficient
questions.question: What does a standing wave on a mismatched antenna feeder actually cause?
options: It changes the impedance the transmitter sees and increases feeder loss
It generates new harmonic frequencies not present in the original signal
It reduces the antenna's efficiency even when the feeder itself is lossless
It has no effect at all as long as the SWR stays below about 3:1
questions.explanation: A standing wave changes the V/I ratio (impedance) seen at the transmitter end of the feeder, and that impedance depends on feeder length. It also raises feeder loss (higher current/voltage peaks). It does NOT generate harmonics — harmonics come from transmitter non-linearity, a completely separate mechanism.

questions.section_name: Standing Waves, SWR, and the Reflection Coefficient
questions.question: A friend says: 'My antenna has a standing wave on the feeder, but the reflected power must be zero because I want a good match.' What is wrong with this statement?
options: SWR meters are incapable of measuring reflected power at all
A standing wave requires non-zero reflected power — SWR 1:1 means none exists
Reflected power is always zero on any correctly installed feeder
A low SWR actually means high reflected power, not a low amount
questions.explanation: A standing wave forms from the superposition of the incident and reflected waves — if there were truly zero reflected power, there would be nothing to superimpose and no standing wave pattern. 'Standing wave present' and 'zero reflected power' are contradictory statements.

questions.question: During a satellite pass using a linear transponder, several other stations' downlinks suddenly get much weaker at the same time, while one particular station's downlink stays strong. What is the most likely cause?
options: The satellite has entered eclipse and its solar panels are temporarily unlit
The transponder has automatically switched to a different downlink band
One uplink is excessively strong, compressing the shared transponder AGC
Doppler shift has moved the weaker stations outside the passband entirely
questions.explanation: A linear transponder has a fixed total output power shared across every signal in its passband. One over-strong uplink compresses the shared AGC, reducing the output level for every OTHER signal — while the strong station's own downlink stays strong. This is a shared-resource problem affecting some signals, not the whole spacecraft.

questions.question: Which scenario would weaken ALL of a satellite's downlinks and its beacon together, rather than affecting just one station's signal?
options: One station transmitting with excessive uplink power to the satellite
Two stations transmitting on very slightly different uplink frequencies
A station using a circularly-polarised uplink antenna for its signal
The satellite entering eclipse, reducing power for the whole spacecraft
questions.explanation: Eclipse (or any reduction in the satellite's own power budget) affects the whole spacecraft, so every downlink and the beacon weaken together, roughly equally. This is the opposite signature to AGC compression from one strong uplink, which weakens other signals while leaving the strong station's own downlink unaffected.
